prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

My desk is cleared of the litter of ages; Before me glitter the fair white pages; My fountain pen is clean and filled, And the noise of the office has long been stilled. Roget’s Thesaurus is at my hand, And I’m ready to do some work that’s grand, Dignified, eminent, great, momentous, Memorable, worthy of note, portentous, Beautiful, paramount, vital, prime, Stirring, eventful, august, sublime. For this is the way, I have read and heard, That authors look for the fitting word. All of the proud ingredients mine To build, like Marlowe, the mighty line. But never a line from my new-filled pen That couldn’t be done by a child of ten. Oh, how did Shelley and how did Keats Weave magic words on the fair white sheets Under conditions that, were they mine, I couldn’t bear? And I’d just resign. Yet Milton wrote passable literature Under conditions I couldn’t endure. Coleridge and Chatterton did their stuff Over a road that I’d christen rough. Wordsworth and—soft!—could it be that they Waited until they had something to say?

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Before, And, Roget

outputs.L1:
My desk is cleared of the litter of ages;  
Before me gleam the fair white pages.  
My fountain pen is clean and filled,  
And the noise of the office has long been stilled.  

Roget’s Thesaurus is close at hand,  
And I am ready to craft something grand:  
Dignified, eminent, great, momentous,  
Memorable, worthy of note, portentous;  
Beautiful, paramount, vital, prime,  
Stirring, eventful, august, sublime.  

For this is the way, I have read and heard,  
That authors search for the fitting word.  
All the proud ingredients are mine  
To build, like Marlowe, the mighty line.  

Yet never a line from my newly filled pen  
Appears that could not be written by a child of ten.  
Oh, how did Shelley, and how did Keats,  
Weave magic words upon fair white sheets  
Under conditions that, were they mine,  
I could not bear—and would simply resign?  

Yet Milton wrote passable literature  
Under conditions I could not endure.  
Coleridge and Chatterton did their work  
Along a road I would have called rough.  

Wordsworth and—soft!—could it be that they  
Waited until they had something to say?
outputs.L2:
My workspace has finally been stripped of its ancient mess.  
In front of me lie bright, untouched sheets of paper.  
My pen has been washed, refilled, and made ready,  
and the office has been quiet for quite some time.  

Roget’s Thesaurus sits within easy reach,  
and I am prepared to create something impressive—  
noble, distinguished, important, weighty,  
unforgettable, remarkable, ominous,  
lovely, supreme, essential, first-rate,  
exciting, significant, majestic, and lofty.  

After all, I have been told—and have read as well—  
that this is how writers discover the perfect word.  
I possess every proud necessity  
for shaping, like Marlowe, a powerful verse.  

Yet my freshly filled pen produces nothing  
that a ten-year-old could not have written.  
How, I wonder, did Shelley and Keats  
set down enchanted language on clean white paper  
while enduring circumstances that, if I faced them,  
would make me give up at once?  

And still, Milton managed to write quite respectable work  
under hardships I would never tolerate.  
Coleridge and Chatterton created their pieces  
while traveling a path I would certainly call difficult.  
Wordsworth, too—and wait—could it be  
that these poets simply delayed writing  
until they actually had something to say?
outputs.L3:
The speaker describes having created the perfect environment for writing. The desk is clean and uncluttered, the pen is filled and ready to use, the office is quiet, and a thesaurus is close at hand. Everything seems carefully arranged to encourage creativity and serious literary work. The speaker appears determined to write something impressive, perhaps even something grand and memorable.

With these preparations in place, the speaker hopes to produce beautiful and important literature. They imagine that, by searching for powerful and unusual words, they might be able to create writing that sounds profound. The thesaurus represents this desire to find striking language and elevate the work through impressive vocabulary.

However, despite having all the necessary tools and ideal conditions, the speaker finds that they cannot produce anything worthwhile. Instead of great poetry or meaningful writing, only simple, childish lines come out. This creates a humorous contrast between the speaker’s high ambitions and their disappointing results.

The speaker then compares their comfortable situation with the difficult lives of famous poets such as Shelley, Keats, Milton, and Coleridge. These writers often created great work despite illness, poverty, personal struggle, or other hardships. Unlike the speaker, they did not necessarily have perfect writing conditions, yet they were able to produce lasting literature.

By the end, the poem suggests that great writing does not come simply from having a tidy desk, a quiet room, a good pen, or access to impressive words. Perfect conditions may help, but they are not enough on their own. What matters more is having something meaningful to express. The poem concludes that true literary power depends less on external comforts and more on depth of thought, feeling, and purpose.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a humorous and self-aware reflection on the difficulties of writing well. The speaker appears to have everything a writer could want: the right tools, a comfortable setting, and the desire to create something impressive. In theory, these ideal conditions should make it possible to produce a great poem. However, the speaker quickly discovers that having the proper materials and the ambition to write does not automatically lead to inspiration or artistic success.

Much of the poem’s humor comes from the speaker’s honest frustration and exaggerated sense of failure. By comparing themselves to famous poets, the speaker highlights the gap between wanting to be great and actually achieving greatness. These comparisons are funny because they show how easy it is for a writer to imagine joining the ranks of literary masters, while also recognizing how difficult that goal really is. The speaker’s self-mockery makes the poem relatable, since many people know the feeling of being prepared to work but still unable to produce anything meaningful.

At the same time, the poem makes a serious point about creativity. It suggests that writing is not simply a matter of having a good pen, a quiet room, or the right atmosphere. Although these things may help, they cannot replace imagination, insight, or genuine emotion. The poem gradually reveals that the real problem is not a lack of equipment or comfort, but a lack of something important to express.

In the end, the poem argues that literary greatness depends less on perfect preparation than on the presence of a meaningful idea. A writer may have every advantage and still produce nothing memorable if there is no real substance behind the words. Through humor and humility, the poem reminds us that great writing comes not from the appearance of being a poet, but from having something worth saying.
outputs.L5:
Before dictionaries became everyday companions, writers searched for better ways to organize their thoughts and choose the right words. And among the most influential tools ever created for this purpose was Roget’s Thesaurus.

Peter Mark Roget believed that words could be grouped not only alphabetically, but by meaning and association. This idea helped people move from a vague thought to a precise expression. Before Roget, finding a stronger synonym or a more fitting phrase often depended on memory or chance. And after his work became widely known, writers, students, and speakers gained a practical guide for expanding their language.

Roget’s contribution reminds us that words are more than definitions. They are connections between ideas, emotions, and experiences. Before we speak or write, we often sense what we want to say but struggle to find the exact form. And with the help of tools like Roget’s Thesaurus, those thoughts can become clearer, richer, and more powerful.
